title: ADP National Employment Report And What the Headli...
content:
ADP National Employment Report And What the Headline Misses About Today’s Labor Market
ADP says private employers added 41,000 jobs in December, framing it as a rebound. But when you slow down and look at where those jobs came from, the picture changes. Nearly all of the net growth came from just two sectors..education and health services (+39,000) and leisure and hospitality (+24,000). Strip those out, and the rest of the economy was net negative. That’s not broad based hiring. That’s a labor market leaning hard on a few non cyclical and high turnover pockets to keep the headline above zero.
Job Quality Matters, And This Mix Isn’t Great
This wasn’t an expansion in high value, productivity driven work. Professional and business services lost 29,000 jobs. Information lost 12,000. Manufacturing fell another 5,000. These are the sectors tied to corporate spending, investment, and future growth. When they’re shrinking while lower wage or institutionally supported sectors are hiring, it usually means firms are protecting margins and pulling back on discretionary labor.
Education and healthcare hiring is structurally supported by demographics and funding flows. Leisure and hospitality hiring is highly sensitive to hours and turnover. Both can add headcount even when demand is slowing, because employers spread fewer hours across more workers or backfill churn. If these jobs disappeared in six months, GDP and tax receipts would barely notice. That’s the uncomfortable truth.
Firm Size Tells The Same Late Cycle Story
ADP highlights a recovery in small business hiring, but the numbers are modest. Small firms added just 9,000 jobs total (4,000 from firms with 1–19 workers, 5,000 from 20–49). Medium sized firms accounted for 34,000 of the 41,000 jobs, while large firms added only 2,000. That’s not aggressive expansion. It looks more like cautious backfilling and selective hiring where firms can’t stretch existing staff any further.
Late in the cycle, large employers typically slow first. That’s exactly what’s showing up here.
Regionally, This Is Not A Healthy Labor Market
One of the most telling details is geographic. The West lost 61,000 jobs, almost entirely from the Pacific region (-59,000). Meanwhile, gains were concentrated in the Northeast and South. In a genuinely strong labor market, you don’t see that kind of regional air pocket without it spreading elsewhere soon after. This looks like stress in high cost, capital intensive regions showing up first.
Wages Don’t Confirm Labor Scarcity 
If labor demand were truly tight, wages would be accelerating broadly. They’re not. Job stayer pay growth stayed flat at 4.4%, unchanged from November. Job changer pay rose to 6.6%, but that’s a narrow group and often late cycle noise..only the most employable workers are moving. More importantly, very small firms (1–19 employees) are seeing just 2.3% pay growth, which is negative in real terms. That’s not what a strong labor market looks like. That’s margin stress showing up in payroll decisions.
What This Report Is Really Saying
This doesn’t read like a strengthening labor market. It reads like a stall. Firms are still hiring just enough to avoid layoffs, but they’re cutting exposure where demand is uncertain. Headcount is being preserved while hours, productivity, and investment quietly soften. That’s classic late cycle behavior.
If conditions worsen, the first cracks won’t show up in the headline number. They’ll show up when leisure and hospitality hiring rolls over, when education and healthcare slow, or when small firms stop backfilling altogether. At that point, the 41,000 will flip fast.
For now, the clean takeaway is simple..this jobs report looks better than the economy actually feels. And historically, that gap doesn’t last very long.

title: If the U.S. ever starts to look politically unpred...
content:
If the U.S. ever starts to look politically unpredictable as the steward of global dollar liquidity, everyone who depends on that plumbing has to adjust. And adjustment, in practice, means self insurance..holding more dollar liquidity, more top tier collateral, more balance sheet protection against funding stress. In the short run, that almost always points to Treasuries..not out of affection for the U.S., but because they remain the cleanest, most functional dollar asset in repo, margining, and crisis liquidity.
That’s why the public show of support for Powell from international central bankers and senior banking figures matters. It wasn’t a statement about policy preferences. It was a signal about institutional continuity. Markets can tolerate tight policy, loose policy, even mistakes. What they struggle with is uncertainty over who ultimately controls the dollar backstop and how decisions get made under stress. Undermining that credibility forces everyone to behave more defensively..hoarding dollars, widening spreads, pulling back liquidity which becomes destabilizing in its own right.
There’s an irony here that often gets missed. A less reliable U.S. doesn’t immediately weaken the dollar system; it can actually increase near term demand for Treasuries as foreign institutions hedge against disruption. But over time, the same fear accelerates efforts to reduce reliance on dollar funding altogether..deeper local currency markets, alternative reserves, internal backstops. Crisis behavior and long term strategy move in opposite directions.
That’s the real logic behind the response you’re seeing. This isn’t about loyalty to any one central banker. It’s about defending the idea that the rules of the dollar system stay boring, predictable, and non political because once that assumption breaks, everyone pays for it.
Actually a less reliable U.S. means Europe needs to buy a lot more Treasuries. They would need to hold more dollar reserves to self-insure against potential loss of FX swap access. 
- 
Joseph Wang

title: The US Dollar just hit its lowest level in nearly ...
content:
The US Dollar just hit its lowest level in nearly four years at $95.6.
The collapse happened right after Trump said the dollar is "doing great" and he's unconcerned about its weakness. 
The irony is brutal, no amount of cheerleading stops a currency selloff when confidence actually breaks.
Three major forces are crushing the dollar simultaneously.
First, policy uncertainty is killing confidence. 
Trump's unpredictable tariff threats and aggressive geopolitical posturing have spooked global investors.
 During his first term, his trade wars depreciated the dollar 10%, now we're watching it happen again. 
Every tariff threat or inflammatory statement causes another wave of dollar selling. 
Beyond trade, Trump's attacks on Fed Chair Powell and signals he might replace him have undermined confidence in US monetary independence. 
When central bank credibility is questioned, capital flees.
Second, rate expectations matter. 
Markets expect the Fed to cut rates at least twice in 2026 while other central banks hold or raise. 
If US rates fall, your dollars earn less, so money flows toward higher yielding currencies like the yen, euro, and Swiss franc. 
Third, the $38 trillion national debt combined with Trump's aggressive spending plans.
Also, shutdown threats have made investors genuinely worried about long term US finances. 
Some European fund managers are actively selling dollar assets because they now view the dollar as a liability rather than a safe haven.
This is a "sell America" rotation where global investors are diversifying out of U.S. assets entirely. 
Gold is surging to record highs as investors flee to alternative safe havens. 
The problem with Trump's dismissal is that he wants a weak dollar for export help.
However, a currency collapse driven by lost confidence is different from controlled depreciation. 
When the dollar crashes this way, import prices spike (gas, electronics, clothes all cost more), foreign investors flee and borrowing costs could skyrocket on $38 trillion of debt. 
The real danger is stagflation, weak growth plus high inflation which is what tariffs plus a collapsing currency actually produces together.
Right now, markets are telling you the U.S. is becoming riskier.
Until Trump stabilizes policy and stops attacking the Fed, expect more dollar weakness ahead.

title: Housing Cracks Don’t Start With Prices They Start ...
content:
Housing Cracks Don’t Start With Prices They Start With Jobs and Confidence
During the GFC, December was often when that stress first became visible in contracts. In December 2007, pending home sales were already down roughly 24% from the prior year, a clear signal that closings were about to weaken further. That wasn’t random timing. The recession officially began that same month, layoffs were rising, credit conditions were tightening, and buyers started worrying that the price they agreed to today might look expensive a few months later if their job or income wasn’t secure. Contracts didn’t fail because prices had already collapsed; they failed because the labor backdrop was turning and confidence was slipping.
That sequencing matters now because unemployment is likely heading higher again, even if it’s moving slowly. The behavioral pattern looks familiar where buyers are cautious, using contracts as probes, double checking payments, insurance, and financing, and walking away when something feels off. The difference versus the GFC is the plumbing. Back then, rising unemployment collided with a credit system that was breaking, forcing mass deleveraging and driving cancellation rates into a completely different regime. Today, cancellations at 16% still look more like a confidence and affordability squeeze than a full credit event. But the line between the two runs straight through the labor market. If job losses continue to broaden and lenders respond by tightening standards, this stops being a simple transaction slowdown and starts to rhyme much more closely with the GFC playbook. That’s the hinge point people should be watching, not just the headline cancellation rate.

title: Texas Manufacturing Is Moving But The Cycle Isn’t
content:
Texas Manufacturing Is Moving But The Cycle Isn’t
Texas manufacturing looked better in January. Production, new orders, and shipments all moved back into positive territory after a weak December. On the surface, it reads like momentum returning.
But when you slow down and read the full report, it feels less like a new cycle beginning and more like the system steadying itself after wobbling late last year.
Output Is Back But The Pipeline Isn’t
Here’s the quiet contradiction sitting under the rebound…
•   Firms are producing and shipping more
•   Order growth is still negative
•   Backlogs are still shrinking
That’s a classic late cycle tension. Companies are busy filling what’s in front of them, but they’re not building depth behind it. Activity improves, but future visibility doesn’t. Things are moving, but the pipeline isn’t thickening. That’s stabilization, not acceleration.
Sentiment Says Relief, Not Confidence 
Business sentiment barely clears neutral. Outlooks improved, but they sound cautious rather than convinced. The tone is telling..less anxiety than December, but no sense of conviction either.
It reads like managers saying..
“The slide stopped… but I’m not ready to lean forward yet.”
That gap between better data and guarded language matters.
Labor Looks Late Cycle, Not Expansionary 
Hiring turned positive again, but hours barely moved. That’s not how companies behave when demand is taking off.
It suggests firms are..
•   Adding selectively
•   Avoiding overtime
•   Preserving flexibility
More telling, fewer firms are even trying to hire at all. And the constraint isn’t a lack of applicants anymore..it’s skills and pay expectations. That’s what a cooling labor market with structural mismatches looks like. Not recession yet. But not growth confidence either.
Pricing Power Is Rising Unevenly
One signal policymakers won’t ignore..firms are getting better at raising prices on finished goods, even as wage pressure cools.
That mix implies…
•   Margins may be improving for firms with pricing power
•   Inflation pressure isn’t gone, just uneven and selective
This is uncomfortable territory. Not hot enough to force action, not cool enough to declare victory.
Recessionary Hints Show Up In The Margins
The most recession sensitive signals don’t live in the headlines they leak out in the details…
•   Backlogs continue to shrink, which often precedes pullbacks in hiring and capex
•   Some firms report customers going out of business and payment terms stretching
•   A meaningful share has frozen capital spending entirely due to uncertainty
Those aren’t expansion behaviors. They’re capital preservation behaviors.
Two Economies Hiding In One Survey
The comments make the divergence clear.
Some firms sound strong…
•   Machinery
•   Equipment
•   Data center linked demand
Others sound strained…
•   Food suppliers losing customers
•   Office and hospitality linked businesses still weak
•   Firms quietly pulling back and protecting cash
That split explains why the averages look fine, but confidence never really follows through.
Capex Is Defensive, Not Exuberant 
Yes, more firms expect to spend in 2026. But where they plan to spend matters.
•   Software
•   Automation
•   Machinery
That’s productivity and risk management spending..not broad demand driven expansion. And alongside that optimism sits a non trivial group that has stopped spending altogether.
The Real Question Going Forward
January tells us the system didn’t break. That’s important.
What it doesn’t tell us is whether demand is rebuilding beneath the surface or whether this was a catch up month after a soft December, helped by timing and seasonality.
February is the tell…
If orders and backlogs start to improve, this becomes the start of a real recovery narrative. If they roll over again, January will look like a pause in a slowdown..not an escape from it.

title: The Quiet Mechanics Behind Europe’s U.S. Equity Ex...
content:
The Quiet Mechanics Behind Europe’s U.S. Equity Exposure
Most of these numbers are reported in market value, not net new purchases. U.S. equities massively outperformed over the last few years, and for long stretches the dollar was strong. Those two forces alone inflate the value of existing foreign holdings. Even if Europeans barely bought anything new, the same shares they already owned would still look much larger on paper.
That distinction matters, because rising exposure isn’t the same thing as rising conviction.
Why This Still Holds Even With A Weaker Dollar Now
This is where people get tripped up. Yes, the dollar has weakened recently and EUR/USD is higher over the past year. But the surge in reported European holdings didn’t happen overnight. It accumulated over multiple years that included long periods of U.S. equity outperformance and earlier dollar strength.
Those valuation gains don’t disappear just because the dollar softens later. Unless assets are sold, the level effect remains. So a falling DXY today doesn’t contradict the story..it just tells you the next leg of returns may look different.
This Isn’t Just About Chasing Returns
U.S. tech and AI crushed European equities. That’s the obvious part. But the quieter driver is that Europe hasn’t given its own capital many compelling alternatives. Energy costs stayed high after the Ukraine shock. Regulation keeps stacking up. Demographics are getting worse, not better. Growth feels capped before it even starts.
So money drifts. Not dramatically. Not ideologically. It drifts toward the place where earnings grow, liquidity is deep, and exits are easy. That’s less a vote for America than a shrug about Europe.
The Plumbing Matters More Than People Think
Another thing that gets missed..a lot of this European ownership runs through funds, custodians, and legal structures in places like Ireland, Luxembourg, or London. That doesn’t always mean European households or governments are the real decision makers. It’s global money wearing a European label.
Which makes the idea that Europe could suddenly dump U.S. equities way overplayed. There’s no red button.
The Real Lever Is Currency Risk, Not Selling
If something shifts, it probably won’t start with mass selling. It’ll start with hedging. For European investors, owning U.S. stocks often also means owning dollars, sometimes unintentionally. When hedging is expensive, they stay unhedged. When the math changes, they adjust.
Those quiet changes in hedge ratios can move FX markets and risk premiums long before anyone talks about selling stocks.
What This Actually Says About The System
At a deeper level, this is about gravity. Global portfolios follow benchmarks. Benchmarks follow market cap. And market cap followed the U.S. That creates a self reinforcing loop where capital concentrates even if no one feels especially bullish.
The real risk isn’t that Europe suddenly leaves. It’s that the marginal buyer slowly fades. Returns flatten, hedges rise, and the U.S. equity risk premium has to do more work on its own.
That’s not a crash story. It’s a regime change story.
My View
This isn’t Europeans making a loud bet on America. It’s global capital responding to performance, structure, and habit. If anything, it’s a quiet signal of how narrow the global growth menu has become.
And those situations rarely end with fireworks. They end with slow shifts that only look obvious in hindsight.

European investors now own a record $10.4 trillion in US stocks.
Ownership has surged +$4.9 trillion, or +91%, over the last 3 years.
Denmark, Finland, France, Germany, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, the UK, now hold ~$5.7 trillion in US equities, or 55% of total European holdings.
By comparison, the rest of the world holds $10.9 trillion.
In other words, European investors now reflect ~49% of all foreign holdings of US equities.

title: Japan's government is warning that it's ready to j...
content:
Japan's government is warning that it's ready to jump into the currency market and buy yen if the currency continues to weaken in what they consider abnormal or speculative ways. 
This warning came from Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi over the weekend and it's sending shockwaves through global markets.
Here's what's been happening. 
The yen has been getting weaker and weaker against the US dollar for months. 
Weaker basically means it takes more yen to buy one dollar.
The yen got dangerously close to 160 yen per dollar which is a level that Japanese officials have basically said is their line in the sand. 
Back in 2024, whenever the yen hit around 160, Japan actually intervened by buying massive amounts of yen to prop it back up. 
They spent nearly $100 billion doing this on four separate occasions. 
That 160 level is now basically understood by the whole market as a trigger point, if the yen gets there, intervention is very possible.
But here's the signal that really spooked traders on Friday.
Reports came out that the Federal Reserve Bank of New York contacted financial institutions asking about current yen exchange rates. 
This type of rate check is basically a red flag in the trading world because it's typically one of the first steps officials take before actually jumping into the market to buy or sell a currency. 
The Fed doing this for Japan is huge because it hints at potential US support for a coordinated intervention something that's quite rare. 
The last time the US and Japan worked together on currency intervention was all the way back in 2011 after the Tohoku earthquake. 
So the market interpreted these rate checks as a strong signal that intervention could be imminent.
Why does this matter to you? 
First, because massive currency moves affect stocks and bonds across the globe. 
When the yen is this weak, it makes Japanese exports more competitive internationally but also makes imports much more expensive. 
This contributes to inflation in Japan, which is already a serious problem.
 A weak yen means Japanese households have less purchasing power everything from oil to raw materials costs more because they have to exchange more yen to buy them. 
Takaichi's government is actually trying to deal with living cost pressures by spending more money and suspending certain taxes.
However, that's actually making the currency situation worse because the government has to borrow more money to pay for it all.
The second reason this matters is because traders have built up record amounts of short positions in the yen, basically bets that it will continue to weaken. 
These short positions are at decade highs, according to the reports. 
If intervention actually happens and the yen strengthens rapidly, all these traders could face massive losses very quickly which could trigger forced selling in other markets and create broader financial stress.
There's also a political angle here. 
Takaichi just took over leadership of the ruling party and is planning a snap election. 
Her administration's spending plans have investors worried about government debt and inflation, so the bond market has been selling off and the yen has been weakening. 
The fact that she's now using strong language about intervention suggests the government is starting to get desperate about the currency situation. 
When elections are coming and your currency is in free fall while your bonds are rising in yield, it creates real pressure to act forcefully.
The timing is also important. 
The New York Fed's rate checks happened on Friday afternoon in the US but Monday morning in Asia typically has very thin trading liquidity because fewer people are around. 
This is the perfect environment for sharp, unpredictable price moves.

title: Japan Isn’t Defending the Yen It’s Enforcing Two W...
content:
Japan Isn’t Defending the Yen It’s Enforcing Two Way Risk
This chart isn’t about Tokyo spending ¥20 trillion to defend the yen. It shows a deterrence strategy, not a fixed line..designed to impose two way risk when depreciation turns disorderly, politically destabilizing, or financially dangerous.
When you align intervention timing, scale, and price reactions with macro conditions and global events, a clear doctrine emerges
What the Chart Really Shows
Japan’s Ministry of Finance intervenes in clusters, not symbolic one offs. Since 2022, action has appeared when USD/JPY accelerated through psychologically important levels..first the mid 140s, later the 150s, and most recently near 160.
Each episode follows the same structure..a large initial strike to shock positioning and reset expectations, followed by smaller follow ups to punish re shorting and reinforce credibility.
Across 2022 and 2024, this totaled roughly ¥24–25 trillion, producing same day yen reversals of 4–6 yen per dollar. The objective was never to permanently reverse the trend. It was to break the belief that yen weakness was a one way trade.
Why This Month Looks Familiar
By late January 2026, USD/JPY was again pressing toward 160, with speculative shorts near decade highs. The response matched prior pre intervention patterns: public warnings against abnormal moves, reports of U.S. officials contacting banks, and sharp intraday yen rebounds without confirmed cash intervention.
This matters because Japan’s interventions work best before dollars are sold. Once dealers and leveraged funds sense coordination risk, positioning starts to unwind on its own.
Not Anti Inflation But Anti Stagflation
Japan is not trying to crush inflation. It spent decades trapped in deflation. The problem is the quality of inflation.
A rapidly weakening yen raises energy and food prices, compresses real wages, and undermines consumption. That import driven inflation is politically toxic and economically destabilizing. Intervening to cap extreme yen weakness protects household purchasing power and preserves the credibility of Japan’s reflation strategy without forcing abrupt monetary tightening.
In that sense, yen intervention is best understood as defending real incomes, not exporters.
Buying Time in a Fragile Global Cycle
Intervention also buys policy flexibility. With global recession risks, heavy debt loads, and volatile bond markets, Japan cannot afford to be forced into aggressive rate hikes just to stabilize the currency.
By dampening overshoots, authorities reduce imported inflation pressure and give the central bank room to normalize policy gradually. The timing..often near global stress points or shifts in U.S. rate expectations suggests interventions act as circuit breakers, not permanent fixes.
Global Coordination, Not Currency War
Japan frames intervention as a response to disorderly moves, aligning with G7 norms rather than mercantilist targeting. Hints of U.S. awareness or quiet support are deliberate. They provide legitimacy and reduce the risk the move is seen as unilateral manipulation.
Historically, coordinated or tacitly approved interventions have been the most effective. This month’s signaling fits that lineage.
My View
Japan’s yen interventions are not about defending a fixed exchange rate. They are about preserving control.
When depreciation becomes one sided, politically dangerous, or financially destabilizing, authorities step in..forcefully and repeatedly to remind markets that extremes will be contested. The strategy works not by stopping the trend, but by breaking the assumption that the trend is risk-free.
As Japan moves through 2026–2027, the effectiveness of this approach will hinge less on how many yen are deployed and more on whether fiscal policy, bond market dynamics, and global coordination continue to support the credibility that makes intervention work.

title: When Lenders Start Saying No Auto Loans Become an ...
content:
When Lenders Start Saying No Auto Loans Become an Early Credit Warning
When auto loan rejections hit the highest level in more than a decade, the headline sounds like consumer stress. But the real signal is credit access tightening, not demand disappearing. The New York Fed’s survey shows rejection rates rising through 2024 and into 2025, with a spike to 15.2% in October 2025 (up from 6.7% in June 2025). And the key historical detail..the previous high was at the start of the series in 2013 meaning this is the worst reading in the entire dataset, not just a normal cycle move.
Why That Matters Now
This is how slowdowns start in the real economy..not with one dramatic recession print, but with lenders quietly saying “no” more often..especially to subprime borrowers, who take the bulk of the rejections. Higher rates, elevated car prices, and rising delinquencies change underwriting fast. Auto is one of the cleanest windows into that because it blends rates, borrower quality, and collateral in one place. You can have markets holding up and headline data still looking fine while the credit channel is already pulling back underneath.
U.S. car loan applications are being rejected at the highest rate in more than a decade

title: China’s Military Purge Hits the Core of Power
content:
China’s Military Purge Hits the Core of Power
China has launched a rare and consequential investigation into Zhang Youxia, Vice Chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC) and long regarded as Xi Jinping’s closest military ally. At the same time, Liu Zhenli, head of the PLA’s Joint Staff Department, has also been placed under investigation. The announcement, made by China’s Ministry of National Defense on January 24, used the standard phrase “suspected serious violations of discipline and law” language that typically signals a decision has already been reached inside the Party.
The significance is hard to overstate. Zhang is only the second sitting CMC vice chairman removed in decades, and his portfolio sat at the intersection of procurement oversight, operational readiness, and strategic modernization. His removal, alongside the PLA’s top operational commander, represents the deepest leadership rupture in China’s military since Xi began his anticorruption campaign.
What Is Confirmed
Multiple independent sources, including Reuters, confirm that both men are under formal investigation. Chinese military commentary has framed the case not merely as corruption, but as a failure of political discipline and loyalty..specifically accusing unnamed senior figures of undermining the “CMC Chairman Responsibility System,” the mechanism that ensures Xi’s personal control over the armed forces. Since 2023, more than 50 senior officers and defense industry executives have been removed, with the campaign expanding into missile forces, procurement bureaus, and state owned defense firms.
The Nuclear Leak Allegation
A Wall Street Journal report claims Zhang leaked sensitive nuclear weapons data to the United States. This allegation has driven much of the public attention, but it remains unverified. Chinese official statements have not referenced espionage, nuclear secrets, or foreign intelligence services, and no second major outlet has independently confirmed the claim. At present, it should be treated as plausible but unproven.
Why Target A Trusted Insider?
Zhang’s closeness to Xi may explain the severity rather than contradict it. Three dynamics likely overlap…
First, the Party appears to be enforcing absolute loyalty at the top of the PLA, signaling that no relationship overrides political discipline. Second, Western defense assessments have already pointed to corruption linked quality failures and false readiness reporting within China’s weapons programs; shielding such failures would be treated as betrayal. Third, with major modernization milestones approaching, Xi appears determined to eliminate autonomous power centers inside the military, even at the cost of short term disruption.
Strategic Implications
In the near term, the purge likely reduces China’s willingness to initiate high risk military action, including a Taiwan invasion, as command disruption and loyalty screening ripple downward. Over time, however, extreme centralization raises different risks..honest reporting is discouraged, initiative is suppressed, and strategic miscalculation becomes more likely.
My View 
This is less a story about espionage than about control. The evidence points to a political security purge aimed at reasserting Party dominance over a military system plagued by corruption, procurement failures, and questionable internal trust. Whether the nuclear leak allegation proves true will matter greatly..but even without it, the removal of Zhang Youxia marks one of the most consequential shifts in China’s military leadership in decades.
What I’d be watching for next is Party expulsions, any shift in official language toward espionage or betrayal, political inspectors replacing operational commanders, and changes in PLA activity around Taiwan.

title: Rick Rieder isn’t an academic or a headline econom...
content:
Rick Rieder isn’t an academic or a headline economist…he’s a markets person who’s spent his entire career watching where things actually break. At BlackRock, he runs global fixed income and sits at the center of rates, credit, and multi asset allocation decisions that move trillions. Before that, he came up through Lehman Brothers and later founded R3 Capital during the financial crisis, which BlackRock acquired. That matters because his instincts were forged in moments when liquidity disappears and refinancing risk suddenly becomes the story.
He’s known less for grand theories and more for understanding transmission and how policy decisions flow through funding markets, credit spreads, housing, and the cost of capital. He’s the kind of investor who cares whether the pipes are shaking, not whether the model looks clean.
Where He Stands On Policy And Why It Resonates Now
On monetary policy, Rieder tends to be pragmatic. He’s generally argued that once rates cross from restrictive into outright constrictive, they start doing damage..especially to housing, small businesses, and credit!dependent parts of the economy. That’s why he’s been more open than many to rate cuts in this phase of the cycle. Not because easy money is good, but because tightening into a refinancing wall is how accidents happen.
On fiscal policy, he’s more measured. You don’t hear him cheering deficits, but you do hear him acknowledge reality that when debt loads are large, the cost of capital matters enormously. His focus is usually on whether policy..monetary or fiscal is making the system more fragile at the margin.
On crypto, his tone has been unusually sober for someone from traditional fixed income. He’s described Bitcoin as durable, has compared it favorably to gold as a store of value, and has treated it as something that belongs in modern portfolios..not as a trade, but as a structural asset. That’s less about hype and more about recognizing how markets evolve.
Why His Name Keeps Coming Up
It’s not hard to see why someone like Trump would be drawn to Rieder. Trump has always favored operators over bureaucrats, people who’ve run real money and understand markets from the inside. Rieder fits that mold..a Wall Street winner, comfortable with scale, and openly critical of policy staying too tight for too long. Picking someone like him would signal a shift toward growth first thinking while still giving markets a sense of credibility.
The bigger point, though is Rieder’s speciality is management during times of stress. He’s spent decades managing through moments when credit turns, liquidity dries up, and policy mistakes get exposed. In a cycle where refinancing risk, credit strain, and term premium are quietly becoming the main characters, that skill set suddenly looks very relevant.
In case you don’t realize what’s coming:
The Chief Investment Officer of BlackRock is now expected to be the next Fed Chair.
And, Trump says cutting rates is a “requirement” for the next Fed Chair and is actively calling for 1% interest rates.
2026 is going to be a wild year. 
- 
The Kobeissi Letter
